description: We're a curious, build-first team excited about the Moon, Mars and space exploration. We love turning NASA data into things people can actually use: clean web apps, clear data visualizations and thoughtfully designed interfaces. We're looking for teammates with skills in coding and web development, graphic design, data management, statistics, or business and economics. Beginners are welcome, curiosity matters most! We communicate in English and Hindi.
summary:
MARGIN: Lunar Ice Explorer is a browser game where you design a lunar orbiter and fly it on a mission to look for water ice near the Moon’s south pole. We built it for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to make spacecraft engineering something anyone can try.

Before launch you work within a budget and trade off mass, power, propulsion, and communications. Then the mission throws real problems at you: getting into orbit, surviving eclipses, losing contact with Earth. The science side draws on NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter references, NASA/JPL Horizons data, and a 3D Moon model derived from NASA data. The gameplay itself is simplified, and it’s labeled that way.

What sets it apart is what happens when you fail. Instead of a game-over screen, a Failure Review Board walks you through what went wrong. You change your design and replay the exact same scenario, so you can see whether your fix worked.

That’s how MARGIN makes systems engineering approachable. Players learn by trying, breaking things, and trying again, and they come away seeing that good space missions depend on careful engineering choices as much as on big discoveries.
details:
Project Details — MARGIN: Lunar Ice Explorer

MARGIN — Lunar Ice Explorer is an interactive, browser-based educational game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by transforming spacecraft systems engineering into an accessible experience where players learn through designing, making decisions, experiencing failures, and improving their spacecraft.

How MARGIN Works

Players take on the role of mission designers tasked with sending an orbiter to investigate potential water ice near the Moon's south pole.

The game follows six stages: Brief, Build, Launch, Fly, Review, and Redesign.

Players can begin with a ready-built spacecraft through Guided Mission or customize their own spacecraft using the Advanced Builder. They select science instruments, power generation, battery storage, propulsion, and communications systems while balancing mass, electrical power, and budget constraints.

After selecting a launch date, players navigate a compressed 75-second mission featuring four engineering challenges, including lunar orbital insertion, eclipses, communication disruptions, and scientific observation opportunities. Their decisions directly affect spacecraft health, energy reserves, scientific progress, and mission success.

MARGIN features an interactive 3D spacecraft visualization, a NASA-derived lunar model, mission telemetry, event-specific audio feedback, and a Failure Review Board that explains the consequences of each decision.

Our Innovation

MARGIN's defining feature is its Failure → Diagnosis → Redesign → Replay system.

Unlike conventional games where failure simply ends an attempt, MARGIN encourages players to investigate why something went wrong. The Failure Review Board identifies affected spacecraft systems, explains engineering trade-offs, and recommends improvements.

Players can then modify their spacecraft and replay the same seeded mission scenario, allowing them to compare outcomes under consistent challenges.

This turns failure into an opportunity for experimentation, critical thinking, and problem-solving.

MARGIN also incorporates scientific uncertainty. Players must consider complementary evidence from different lunar instruments rather than assuming that a single measurement confirms the presence of extractable water ice.

NASA Data and Scientific Accuracy

We integrated authentic NASA resources into the experience:

  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO): Scientific information about instruments including LEND, Diviner, LAMP, LOLA, LROC, Mini-RF, and CRaTER.
  • NASA/JPL Horizons: Cached Earth–Moon distance and communication light-time data for three selectable dates in 2027.
  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio: A detailed lunar 3D model derived from LRO observations.
  • NASA Moon Fact Sheet: Reference values used to calculate orbital speed, orbital period, and maximum eclipse duration for a simplified circular lunar orbit.

We deliberately distinguish real scientific references from illustrative gameplay assumptions. Spacecraft component costs, simulated performance, mission events, and scoring are simplified for educational purposes. MARGIN is not intended to replace professional mission-design software.

Technologies and Development Tools

MARGIN was built using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, CSS, and the Web Audio API.

We used GitHub for version control, GitHub Actions for automated testing and deployment, and GitHub Pages to publish the playable experience.

AI development assistants, including GitHub Copilot, Claude, and ChatGPT, supported aspects of programming, research interpretation, debugging, documentation, and design iteration. Our team reviewed and refined the implementation, including correcting engineering-model inconsistencies and adding regression tests.

The project is entirely software-based and requires no specialized hardware. It can be accessed through a modern web browser.

Benefits and Intended Impact

MARGIN aims to make space engineering more understandable and engaging for students, aspiring engineers, educators, and anyone curious about space exploration.

Rather than memorizing engineering principles, players experience how constraints interact. They discover why increased scientific capability may require more energy, why battery storage differs from power generation, and how a small design compromise can influence an entire mission.

Our team also considered accessibility, beginner-friendly onboarding, scientific credibility, browser performance, replayability, and the importance of explaining failures clearly.

The intended impact is to encourage interest in STEM education while strengthening systems thinking, analytical reasoning, and informed decision-making.

Ultimately, MARGIN demonstrates that successful space exploration is not just about reaching a destination—it is about understanding every decision that makes the journey possible.

Play MARGIN: https://abidandey.github.io/margin-/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/abidandey/margin-/
